title: The Ang Pow Question
teaser: Your longest-serving employee asks, quietly, after closing: "Boss, is the shop actually doing okay? People are talking."
concept: Running a business without clinging to the fixed mark of 'towkay who always has it under control.'

start.text: She's worked the counter for eleven years, since before your father handed you the keys. She's not asking to gossip. She's asking because her name is on the payroll too.
start.reflection: Is keeping up appearances actually protecting the shop, or just protecting your own sense of being the boss who has everything under control?

choices.label: "Honestly — it's tight. Here's exactly where we stand."

ending_appearance.text: She nods and goes back to closing up. Three weeks later she gives notice for a job with steadier hours. In the exit conversation she mentions, gently, that she'd have stayed and helped if she'd known how bad things really were — she just didn't feel trusted with the truth.
ending_appearance.insight: The sutra's 'mark of self' isn't only personal vanity — for a towkay it can be the fixed identity of 'the boss who has it handled.' Protecting that mark cost you the one person who might have helped you handle it.

ending_honest.text: She's quiet for a moment, then starts talking through ideas — a supplier she knows who'd extend better terms, a slow weekday she thinks you could close early. None of it fixes everything. All of it helps, and none of it would have come if you'd kept performing certainty.
ending_honest.insight: Giving her the real picture, without dwelling on your pride as towkay, turned an employee into a partner in solving the problem. That's the sutra's teaching on giving fully, without a fixed idea of what you have to protect in the giving.
